newsitem.title: UK: GOOD NEWS FOR THE STINGY - CHEAPER WHISKY IS SAFER.
newsitem.headline: GOOD NEWS FOR THE STINGY - CHEAPER WHISKY IS SAFER.

text.p: Don't get offended if friends present you with a bottle of cheap whisky, Dutch researchers suggested on Friday -- they probably care for your health.
They found that all whiskies they tested contained cancer-causing chemicals, and the more expensive the brand, the more of the chemicals it had.
Scotch malts are the worst offenders because the smoky peat used to smooth the taste carries high levels of the chemicals, which are present in all smoked or burnt foods.
"Carcinogenic polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) were present in all whisky brands," Jos Kleinjans and colleagues at the University of Maastricht wrote in a letter to the Lancet medical journal.
Whisky drinkers are known to be more likely to develop bowel, mouth and throat cancers and Kleinjans decided to analyse various whisky brands to see if he could find out why.

His team of health risk analysts and toxicologists tested 18 brands of whisky. Smoky Scotch single malts such as Laphroaig and Oban contained large amounts of PAHs, while some Irish whiskies such as Jameson, made without peat, had low amounts.
American whiskies and bourbons fell in the middle.
The team concluded that concentrations of PAHs in whiskies were low and were probably not responsible for the higher rates of cancer in whisky drinkers.
"But it is good to know that for minimising health risk, the cheaper buy is the better buy," they concluded.
Britain's Scotch Whisky Association immediately leapt to the defence of the tipple.
"Quite frankly, we regard this letter as nothing other than an irresponsible piece of sensationalism," spokesman Campbell Evans said.
He said burnt toast contained more PAHs than a glass of malt whisky.
"People should bear in mind that if they drink malt whisky in moderation they won't be doing themselves harm. They'll be doing themselves a lot of good."
Moderate consumption of spirits or wine has been found to decrease deaths from heart disease.
